title: JavaScript Core: Types, Scope, Hoisting and Closures
objectives: Distinguish primitive and reference types and predict copying and comparison behaviour.
Explain var, let and const in terms of scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
Describe how closures capture variables and use them for private state.
Explain how the value of 'this' is decided and how arrow functions differ.
Answer classic output-prediction questions on coercion and equality.
definition: JavaScript is a dynamically typed language with seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and objects, which are passed around by reference. Scope decides where a variable is visible; a closure is a function together with the variables from its surrounding scope that it keeps alive after that scope has finished executing.

theory.heading: Primitive versus reference values
theory.body: Primitives are immutable and compared by value: copying a number copies the value. Objects, arrays and functions are reference values: a variable holds a reference, so assigning it to another variable makes both point to the same object. This explains why mutating an array inside a function is visible to the caller, and why Angular's OnPush change detection (Day 20) relies on replacing objects rather than mutating them.
points: typeof null is 'object' (a historical bug); use value === null to test for null.
=== compares without type coercion; == coerces (for example '5' == 5 is true).
Two different objects are never ===, even with identical contents.
const prevents reassignment of the variable, not mutation of the object it points to.

theory.heading: Scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone
theory.body: JavaScript has global, function and block scope. During the creation phase of an execution context, declarations are registered before code runs (hoisting). var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined, and are function-scoped. let and const are block-scoped and hoisted but not initialised, so accessing them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError: that window is the temporal dead zone. Function declarations are hoisted with their body; function expressions follow the rules of the variable they are assigned to.
points: Prefer const by default, let when reassignment is needed, avoid var.
Block scope makes let safe in loops: each iteration gets a fresh binding.
Lexical scope: a function sees variables where it is defined, not where it is called.

theory.heading: Closures
theory.body: When a function is created, it keeps a reference to its lexical environment. If an inner function outlives its outer function (it is returned, stored or used as a callback), the variables it uses stay alive. Closures give private state without classes, power factories, memoisation, debouncing and partial application, and are everywhere in callback-based Node.js code and RxJS operators.
points: Data privacy: variables in the outer function cannot be reached from outside.
Function factories: makeMultiplier(3) returns a function that remembers 3.
Common bug: var in a loop with setTimeout prints the final value for every callback.
Memory: closures keep captured variables alive, so avoid capturing large objects unnecessarily.

theory.heading: How 'this' is determined
theory.body: For normal functions, 'this' is decided by how the function is called, not where it is written. A method call obj.fn() sets this to obj; a plain call fn() gives undefined in strict mode (modules and classes are strict); new sets this to the new object; call, apply and bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions do not have their own 'this' and use the one from the enclosing scope, which is why they are used for callbacks inside class methods in Angular components.
points: Losing 'this': passing obj.method as a callback detaches it from obj.
Fix with an arrow function, bind, or a class field arrow function.
Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors and have no arguments object.

theory.heading: Type coercion pitfalls
theory.body: Operators coerce operands: + concatenates if either side is a string, while -, * and / convert to numbers. Falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN; everything else, including '0', [] and {}, is truthy. NaN is the only value not equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN. The nullish coalescing operator ?? only falls back on null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and ''.
points: Optional chaining user?.address?.city avoids errors on missing objects.

example.title: A closure that keeps state private
example.body: createCounter returns two functions that share the same count variable. Nothing outside can modify count directly, and each call to createCounter creates a separate, independent count. This is the module pattern that predates classes and ES modules.

use_cases.title: Encapsulated modules
use_cases.description: Factories and module patterns expose a small API while keeping helper state private.

use_cases.title: Event handlers and callbacks
use_cases.description: Handlers remember the item or ID they were created for, for example a click handler per list row.

use_cases.title: Memoisation and caching
use_cases.description: A wrapper function keeps a private cache Map so repeated calls with the same input are fast.

use_cases.title: Middleware configuration
use_cases.description: Express middleware factories such as rateLimit({ max: 100 }) return a function that closes over the options.

demonstration.description: Predict the output of the classic loop question. With var there is one shared i, and the callbacks run after the loop finishes. With let each iteration has its own binding, so each closure captures a different value.
demonstration.output:
var 3
var 3
var 3
let 0
let 1
let 2

takeaways: Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared by reference and compared by identity.
var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined; let and const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone.
A closure keeps its outer variables alive and is the basis of private state and factories.
'this' depends on the call site, except in arrow functions, which inherit it lexically.
Use === and ?? to avoid surprising coercion.

interview.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
interview.answer: var is function-scoped, can be redeclared and is hoisted as undefined. let and const are block-scoped, cannot be redeclared in the same scope and are in the temporal dead zone until declared. const cannot be reassigned, though an object it refers to can still be mutated.
interview.explanation: Mention scope, hoisting, the TDZ and the const-mutation nuance; those four points separate a complete answer from a partial one.

interview.question: What is a closure? Give a practical use.
interview.answer: A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables in the scope where it was created, which it can still use after that scope has returned. Uses include private state (a counter or bank account), function factories, memoisation and configured middleware.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want a definition plus a real use. Writing a small factory on the whiteboard is the strongest proof.

interview.question: What does this code print: console.log(typeof null, typeof [], typeof NaN)?
interview.answer: 'object object number'. typeof null is a long-standing quirk, arrays are objects (use Array.isArray), and NaN is of type number.
interview.explanation: These quirks are favourite screening questions; follow up by naming the correct checks (=== null, Array.isArray, Number.isNaN).

interview.question: Why might 'this' be undefined inside a method used as a callback, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: Passing obj.method as a callback calls it as a plain function, so 'this' is undefined in strict mode. Fix it by wrapping in an arrow function (() => obj.method()), using obj.method.bind(obj), or defining the method as an arrow-function class field.
interview.explanation: This shows you understand that 'this' is set at call time; in Angular it appears with setTimeout or third-party callbacks inside components.

interview.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? How?
interview.answer: Yes. A long-lived closure, such as an event listener or an interval callback that is never removed, keeps every captured variable reachable, including large objects or DOM nodes, so they cannot be garbage-collected. Remove listeners, clear intervals and unsubscribe when the owner is destroyed.
interview.explanation: Linking this to Angular (unsubscribing in ngOnDestroy or using takeUntilDestroyed) shows senior-level awareness.

practice.title: Private bank accounts with closures
practice.objective: Use closures to hold private state that can only be changed through a controlled API.
practice.statement: Implement createAccount(initial) that returns an object with deposit, withdraw, getBalance and getHistory functions. The balance and history must live in closure variables, not object properties. Then process commands, one per line: 'open <name> <amount>', 'deposit <name> <amount>', 'withdraw <name> <amount>', 'balance <name>' and 'history <name>'. Print output only for balance, history and errors.
practice.input_format: One command per line. Names are single words; amounts are numbers. Blank lines are ignored.
practice.output_format: balance prints '<name>: <balance>'. history prints '<name>: ' followed by entries such as +50 and -30 separated by spaces, or '<name>: no transactions'. Errors print '<name>: unknown account', '<name>: already exists', '<name>: invalid amount' (amount not greater than 0) or '<name>: insufficient funds'.

example.input:
open alice 100
deposit alice 50
withdraw alice 500
withdraw alice 30
balance alice
history alice

constraints: Opening balance is a number of at least 0 and is not recorded in history.
A failed deposit or withdrawal does not change the balance or history.
Accounts are independent: each open creates a new closure.
explanation: createAccount declares balance and history inside the function; the returned methods close over them, so no outside code can touch them directly.
deposit and withdraw validate the amount first (!(amount > 0) also rejects NaN) and return an error string instead of changing state.
getHistory returns a copy so callers cannot mutate the private array.
A Map stores one account object per name; each open call creates a fresh closure with its own state.
The command loop prints balances, history and any error string returned by the account.

quiz.question: What does this hoisting example print?
options: A ReferenceError on the first line
quiz.explanation: var a is hoisted and initialised to undefined. let b is in the temporal dead zone until its declaration, so reading it throws a ReferenceError.

quiz.question: Which statement about closures is correct?
options: Closures are created only by calling bind()
An inner function keeps access to variables of its outer scope even after the outer function returns
A closure copies the outer variables' values at creation time and never sees later changes
Closures only exist when a function is declared with the 'function' keyword
quiz.explanation: Closures keep a live reference to the outer environment, so they see the current value of captured variables, and arrow functions form closures too.

quiz.question: What do these || and ?? expressions print?
quiz.explanation: || falls back on any falsy value, including 0. ?? only falls back on null or undefined, so it keeps 0.

quiz.question: Inside a class method you call setTimeout(this.save, 1000), and save() throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined'. What is the best fix?
options: Pass an arrow function: setTimeout(() => this.save(), 1000)
Change const to let in the class
quiz.explanation: Passing this.save detaches the method from the instance. An arrow function keeps the lexical 'this' and calls save as a method.

quiz.question: What does this array reference example print?
quiz.explanation: Arrays are reference values: copy points to the same array, so the push is visible through list and both variables are identical.
